# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria is a highly centralized system divided into primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, governed by the Federal Ministry of Education. Primary education is compulsory and free, typically lasting six years starting around age five. It covers core subjects including Mathematics, English, and indigenous languages (Hausa, Yoruba, or Igbo), with a focus on continuous assessment rather than formal exams. Secondary education follows a "6-3-3-4" structure, comprising six years of primary, three years of Junior Secondary School (JSS), three years of Senior Secondary School (SSS), and four years of university. The SSS culminates in examinations administered by the West African Examination Council (WAEC) or the National Examination Council (NECO), where grades like Credit (C4–C6) are required for university admission. The system includes federal, state, and private institutions, though disparities in funding, infrastructure, and teacher quality persist, particularly in rural areas and in the North.
Tertiary education in Nigeria consists of universities, polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education, with the government holding majority control. Admission is primarily based on the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME), with a minimum cut-off mark of 180. While public universities are tuition-free, they face challenges regarding infrastructure, low teacher salaries, and high student-to-teacher ratios. Vocational education is overseen by the National Board for Technical Education and includes apprenticeships, though it often suffers from outdated curricula and a lack of industry alignment. Despite efforts to improve literacy and access, challenges such as insecurity, poverty, gender barriers, and political instability continue to hinder the quality and equity of the Nigerian education system.
